title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: A pharmaceutical P&L is an abstraction until you follow a single molecule from the bioreactor or apheresis suite to the infusion chair and the pharmacy benefit manager's rebate ledger.
epigraph.author: Specialty Biopharma Field Notes

web_blocks.html: Gilead Sciences is a focused drugmaker targeting viral diseases, cancer, and liver disorders. In FY2025, it posted $29,443 million in total revenue (+2% YoY) and over $28,000 million in base product sales excluding Veklury (+4% YoY) [1, 3]. Growth sped up sharply in Q3 2026. Total product sales rose 13% YoY to $8.3 billion, while base sales (excluding Veklury) jumped 16% YoY to $8.2 billion [4]. That marked Gilead's fastest core growth in over ten years. Management raised full-year 2026 product sales guidance to $31.0–$31.3 billion ($30.7–$31.0 billion excluding Veklury) [4].

web_blocks.takeaway: HIV remains >71% of product sales and the primary cash engine, but Trodelvy (+42% YoY) and Livdelzi (+93% YoY) are finally scaling into meaningful secondary growth pillars in 2026.

web_blocks.html: To ground these numbers in real care, each of the five segments follows one patient from clinic visit to manufacturing and payment.

1. HIV Treatment & Prevention (Biktarvy & Yeztugo): Picture a 34-year-old newly diagnosed HIV-1 patient in Atlanta visiting a 340B clinic. The doctor prescribes Biktarvy (bictegravir 50 mg / emtricitabine 200 mg / TAF 25 mg). It is a single small pill made at Gilead's chemical plants and shipped via wholesale and specialty pharmacies. Biktarvy pairs an unboosted integrase blocker with a high resistance barrier and a bone-safe TAF backbone. Patients need no genetic screen or viral-load wait and can start the same day. That ease of use helped Biktarvy reach $14.3 billion in FY2025 sales and $4.1 billion in Q3 2026 alone [3, 4]. Payment flows through commercial plans (with copay cards), Medicaid, Ryan White ADAP, or Medicare Part D. Gilead absorbs statutory rebates, 340B discounts, and Part D catastrophic costs [1]. For prevention, picture a 26-year-old at high HIV risk who struggles with daily pills or stigma. Under CDC guidelines [16], the clinic gives Yeztugo (lenacapavir). The patient takes two starter pills on Days 1–2 and gets two small abdominal shots in the clinic, then returns every 26 weeks [5]. Yeztugo hit $305 million in Q3 2026 sales, pushing Gilead's total PrEP book to a $4 billion annual pace [4]. Priced near $28,000 a year in the U.S., it is also licensed royalty-free to generic makers like Dr. Reddy's at ~$40/year in 120 lower-income countries [17]. Yeztugo removes 363 days of daily pills each year [6, 7].

2. Oncology — Antibody-Drug Conjugates (Trodelvy): Picture a 52-year-old woman in Chicago with newly metastatic triple-negative breast cancer (mTNBC). This fast-growing tumor lacks estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptors. Before June 2026, her doctor had to start with generic chemo and wait for progression before using Trodelvy. After the June 24, 2026 FDA approvals from ASCENT-03 and ASCENT-04 [8], the doctor checks PD-L1 status first. If CPS ≥ 10, she gets Trodelvy + pembrolizumab (Keytruda); if PD-L1-negative, she gets Trodelvy alone. Trodelvy links a Trop-2 antibody to SN-38, an active chemo payload, delivering it directly to tumor cells and nearby tissue. It ships as a vial and is infused by IV on Days 1 and 8 of a 21-day cycle in an outpatient clinic. Clinics bill it under the medical benefit via Medicare Part B or commercial plans while managing side effects like low white blood cells and diarrhea. First-line use lifted Trodelvy sales 42% YoY to $506 million in Q3 2026 [4].

3. Oncology — Autologous Cell Therapy (Kite: Yescarta, Tecartus & Anito-cel): Unlike pills or off-the-shelf vials, Kite's CAR-T drugs are custom living therapies made for one patient at a time. Picture a 61-year-old patient with relapsed large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) at MD Anderson Cancer Center. First, the patient undergoes leukapheresis, a blood draw that collects T-cells. Couriers ship those frozen cells under strict tracking to a Kite plant in El Segundo, Frederick, or Hoofddorp. Over 14 to 17 days, Kite uses a viral vector to add a CD19 receptor, grows millions of cells, runs safety tests, and ships the bag back. After mild chemo, the patient receives one Yescarta infusion and is watched for cytokine release syndrome (CRS). Hospitals bill via inpatient DRG payments, Medicare add-on payments, or commercial case rates above $400,000 per dose. Through the April 2026 Arcellx deal [9], Kite is applying this same plant network to anito-cel for multiple myeloma ahead of a December 23, 2026 FDA PDUFA date [10].

4. Liver Disease (Livdelzi, Epclusa, Vemlidy, Hepcludex): Picture a 55-year-old woman in Boston with Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC), an autoimmune liver disease. Generic UDCA has failed to control her liver enzymes or her severe itching. Her specialist prescribes Livdelzi (seladelpar), a once-daily oral pill gained in the $4.3 billion CymaBay deal [11]. Unlike older second-line drugs that often worsened itching, Livdelzi lowers alkaline phosphatase (ALP) while easing itch. That edge drove Q3 2026 sales up 93% YoY to $203 million [4]. Specialty pharmacies ship Livdelzi under Medicare Part D and commercial plans, alongside Gilead's mature HCV cures (Epclusa/Harvoni), chronic HBV drug Vemlidy, and HDV drug Hepcludex.

5. Veklury (Remdesivir — Acute Antiviral): Finally, picture a 76-year-old immune-weakened patient admitted to a local hospital with COVID-19 pneumonia and low oxygen. The hospital pharmacy stocks Veklury as an IV drug given over 3 to 5 days under bundled inpatient DRG pay. As hospital COVID-19 admissions fell, Veklury shrank from a $5.6 billion peak to $911 million in FY2025 [3] and ~$300 million guided for FY2026 [4]. Today it acts as a small seasonal buffer rather than a core growth driver.

Geographic Mix, Trade Tariffs & FX Exposure: Gilead's revenue base remains heavily U.S.-centric. In Q3 2026, U.S. product sales totaled $6,361 million (76.7% of $8,289 million total product sales), while Europe contributed $1,058 million (12.8%) and Rest of World contributed $869 million (10.5%) [4]. Because Gilead manufactures key active ingredients and biologics across U.S. and European (Ireland/Netherlands) sites, its Q3 2026 Form 10-Q explicitly flags changes in U.S. trade policies, including tariffs, and new U.S. tax legislation alongside foreign-currency translation swings as material operational risks. Meanwhile, Q3 2026 also brought FDA approval of Bixlenvo (bictegravir 75 mg / lenacapavir 50 mg) for virologically suppressed HIV patients and a definitive agreement to acquire PepStar Therapeutics (oral IL-23R inhibitor HCXT-2001) in inflammation [4].

book_paragraphs: If you open Gilead's income statement, you see $29.4 billion of revenue in 2025 and a trajectory toward $31 billion in 2026. But a spreadsheet cannot tell you how differently each of Gilead's five businesses actually works in the real world. One segment sells a tiny daily pill at an 85%-plus gross margin; another manufactures a living, bespoke cell therapy for a single human being in a sterile cleanroom; and a third sells an IV vial directly into hospital emergency rooms. Let's walk through all five segments on the ground, because understanding the physical and reimbursement mechanics of each one explains everything about Gilead's margins, its risks, and its capital needs.

Start with the crown jewel: HIV, which still accounts for roughly 71% of Gilead's product sales—$20.8 billion in 2025, accelerating 18% year-over-year to $6.2 billion in the third quarter of 2026 alone. Picture a 34-year-old patient in Atlanta who just tested positive for HIV. Twenty-five years ago, that patient faced a handful of toxic pills every few hours. Today, their infectious-disease doctor writes one prescription: Biktarvy. It is a single small-molecule tablet combining three drugs—bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide—that can be started the very same day without waiting for genetic screening. Biktarvy alone generated $14.3 billion in 2025 and $4.1 billion in Q3 2026, commanding 53% of the U.S. HIV treatment market.

Now shift from treatment to prevention. Imagine a 26-year-old at high risk of HIV who knows that taking a daily prevention pill—even Truvada or Descovy—carries stigma and adherence fatigue. Under CDC guidelines updated in late 2025, their clinic can now offer Yeztugo, Gilead's twice-yearly lenacapavir injection. After two initiation tablets, the patient receives two small subcutaneous injections in the abdomen and walks out protected for six full months. That convenience is why Yeztugo hit $305 million in Q3 2026 alone—on pace for roughly $1 billion in its first full calendar year—and pushed Gilead's total HIV prevention business to a $4 billion annualized run rate.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Compare the unit economics of Biktarvy and Yescarta: Biktarvy is stamped out in high-volume chemical plants at pennies per tablet and shipped through wholesalers. Yescarta requires a dedicated bioreactor batch for every single patient. One scales effortlessly; the other scales with cleanrooms, couriers, and hospital beds.

book_subsections.title: Oncology's Two Very Different Engines: Trodelvy vs. Kite Cell Therapy
paragraphs: Gilead's oncology business, roughly 11% of product sales in 2025, actually runs on two completely different operational models. The first is Trodelvy, an antibody-drug conjugate. Picture a 52-year-old woman in Chicago diagnosed with metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. Until June 2026, her oncologist had to start her on generic chemotherapy and wait for the cancer to progress before using Trodelvy. After the FDA approved Trodelvy for first-line use based on the ASCENT-03 and ASCENT-04 trials, she can now receive Trodelvy—either alone or paired with Merck's Keytruda—right from Day One. Trodelvy is infused in an outpatient cancer clinic on Days 1 and 8 of a 21-day cycle, and billed under the medical benefit. That first-line expansion is why Trodelvy sales jumped 42% year-over-year to $506 million in Q3 2026.

The second oncology engine is Kite's autologous CAR-T cell therapy—Yescarta and Tecartus—which is one of the most logistically complex therapies in modern medicine. Picture a 61-year-old lymphoma patient at MD Anderson. First, a machine draws the patient's blood to harvest their T-cells. Those cells are frozen and flown under strict chain-of-identity tracking to a Kite manufacturing plant in California, Maryland, or the Netherlands. Over two weeks, technicians genetically engineer those T-cells to hunt CD19-positive cancer cells, multiply them, test them for sterility, and ship them back to Houston. After preparatory chemotherapy, the patient receives a one-time infusion priced north of $400,000. It is a clinical miracle, yet Kite's sales fell 7% in 2025 and mid-teens in 2026 as rivals like BMS's Breyanzi and J&J's Carvykti took share—which is precisely why Gilead bought Arcellx for $7.8 billion to bring anito-cel into multiple myeloma.

book_subsections.title: Liver Disease and the Fading Veklury Buffer
paragraphs: Rounding out the portfolio are Liver Disease ($3.2 billion in 2025) and Veklury ($911 million in 2025). In liver disease, Gilead's mature Hepatitis C cures (Epclusa, Harvoni) are slowly declining, but Livdelzi—acquired from CymaBay in 2024—has injected fresh growth. For a 55-year-old woman with Primary Biliary Cholangitis whose liver enzymes remain elevated and whose skin itches relentlessly on generic UDCA, Livdelzi is a once-daily oral pill that lowers alkaline phosphatase while actually calming pruritus. That clinical edge propelled Livdelzi to $203 million in Q3 2026, up 93% year-over-year.

Finally, Veklury—remdesivir—sits in hospital pharmacies for severely ill COVID-19 patients. As hospitalizations have normalized, Veklury has dropped from $5.6 billion in 2021 to an expected $300 million in 2026. For you and me, that decline is actually clarifying: Veklury is no longer distorting the P&L, leaving a clean view of Gilead's ~16% base-business growth engine.

One geographic reality worth keeping in mind is how concentrated Gilead remains in the United States: in Q3 2026, $6.36 billion of Gilead's $8.29 billion in product sales—nearly 77%—came from U.S. clinics and pharmacies, with Europe at 12.8% and Rest of World at 10.5%. That domestic concentration insulates Gilead somewhat from emerging-market currency swings, yet it also magnifies exposure to U.S. drug-pricing policy, IRA negotiations, and potential cross-border pharmaceutical tariffs given Gilead's European manufacturing footprint. At the same time, the pipeline keeps broadening: in Q3 2026, the FDA approved Bixlenvo, a new single-tablet regimen pairing bictegravir and lenacapavir for switch patients, and Gilead agreed to acquire PepStar Therapeutics' oral IL-23R program in inflammation.
